title: Quashawam
summary: Quashawam was a Montaukett Sunksquaw whose life unfolded during warfare, succession struggles, and colonial land pressure in the seventeenth century. As a daughter of Wyandanch and Wuchikittawbut, she carried Montaukett authority through diplomacy, court orders, testimony, and land transactions from Montauk and Shinnecock country to Jamaica and colonial courts.
content:
Quashawam was a seventeenth-century Montaukett sunksquaw and daughter of Wyandanch and Wuchikittawbut whose authority appears in diplomacy, court orders, testimony, and land transactions. Her birth date is not established; she disappears from colonial records after 1666, and testimony given in July 1669 reported that she had died by then.

Quashawam is known mostly through surviving records produced by English and Dutch colonial officials, town clerks, and land claimants. Those records preserve Quashawam's political role, but they also reflect colonial attempts to force Native authority into deed-making systems that served colonial land transfer.1

Montaukett and Shinnecock Leadership

On February 11, 1663/64, English witnesses recorded an agreement naming Quashawam as a leading sunksquaw over Montaukett and Shinnecock affairs. The agreement says the Shinnecock would recognize her authority, sets limits on conflict between Montaukett and Shinnecock people, and lays out a line of succession after her death.1

That document does not mean that Native leadership worked exactly as the English described it. Strong and Karabag explain that colonial officials preferred a single hereditary leader whose name could be attached to land agreements, while Native communities often used more flexible forms of authority based on kinship, diplomacy, war leadership, and local responsibility.1

John Scott and Land Records

The same day, Quashawam granted power of attorney to John Scott, authorizing him to pursue payment for Long Island lands already taken or bought without full payment, and to handle additional land transactions.1 Strong and Karabag caution that Scott was an ambitious colonial land speculator, so the surviving document should not be treated as a simple record of Quashawam's wishes without considering the pressure around her.1

On February 25, 1663/64, Scott acted in a Jamaica, Queens transaction that included a benefit for Quashawam: twelve looking glasses were to be delivered to her by early March.1 The record shows her name and claimed authority reaching beyond Montauk at a moment when English and Dutch influence on Long Island was shifting.

Later Records

In June 1665, the court at Southold required East Hampton to continue an annual payment owed to the Montauk sunksquaw, showing Quashawam defending obligations attached to earlier land agreements.1

In October 1665, Governor Richard Nicolls and Long Island leaders addressed the colonial fiction of a single superior sachem over Long Island. The ruling ended that title while also addressing Montaukett boundaries, grazing rights, crop damage, and payments owed to Quashawam.1

By 1665-1666, Strong and Karabag place Quashawam and her Pequot husband in a Native village on the west side of Three Mile Harbor in East Hampton. In the Catawamuck, or Crab Meadow, dispute, Richard Smith sought her testimony about whether Wyandanch had received the land from Nasseconset. Quashawam supported the memory of the transfer but said she did not know the details and had no written record.1

What is uncertain

Later local traditions say Quashawam was captured on her wedding night and sometimes call her Heather Flower. Strong and Karabag treat those details as later folklore or literary tradition rather than seventeenth-century documentation.1 The history therefore uses Quashawam, the name preserved in records, and does not present Heather Flower as a documented Native name.

Quashawam disappears from colonial records after 1666. Ninigret testified in July 1669 that Wyandanch's daughter was dead, but the exact date, place, and circumstances of her death are not available in the reviewed sources.1

References

  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, Vol. VI, 1983; includes transcriptions from William S. Pelletreau, ed., The Second Book of Records of the Town of Southampton.
  • John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island, Syracuse University Press, 2001.
  • John A. Strong, "Wyandanch and the Dispossession of Indian Land on Long Island, New York: Grand Sachem, Puppet, or Culture Broker?"
  • Court of Assizes ruling on superior sachem authority, October 3-4, 1665, as discussed in John A. Strong scholarship and Suffolk County Archaeological Association Vol. 49, No. 1, Winter 2023.
why_this_matters: Quashawam makes Native women's leadership visible in Long Island records that are often told only through male sachems and colonial deed makers. Her biography also shows how colonial governments tried to simplify Native authority for land transactions, while Native kinship, diplomacy, and community responsibility were more complex.
